subject: English
topic: Error Detection II — Identify the Grammatically Incorrect Part (W11 B2)

questions.stem:
Find the part with a grammatical error:
(A) The committee has / (B) decided to postpone / (C) their meeting / (D) until next week.
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Committee' is a collective noun treated as singular in formal British/Indian English when acting as one body. The verb 'has' (Part A) is correct for singular. Therefore, the pronoun should be singular 'its' not plural 'their'. Error: 'their meeting' → should be 'its meeting'. Trap: Students often treat collective nouns as plural because committees are made up of people, but in formal usage (standard for SSC), they take singular pronouns.

questions.stem:
Find the part with a grammatical error:
(A) He is one of those / (B) students who / (C) always completes / (D) their homework on time.
questions.explanation: C is correct. In 'one of those + plural noun + who', the relative pronoun 'who' refers back to the PLURAL noun ('students'), not to 'one'. Therefore the verb must be plural: 'complete', not 'completes'. Error: 'always completes' → should be 'always complete'. Full correct: 'He is one of those students who always complete their homework on time.' 'Their' (Part D) agrees with 'students' (plural) and is correct. Trap: Most candidates see 'one of those students' and think the verb should agree with 'one' (singular) → adding -s. But 'who' takes its number from its antecedent 'students'.

questions.stem:
Find the part with a grammatical error:
(A) Neither the manager / (B) nor the employees / (C) was present / (D) at the meeting.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Rule: 'Neither...nor' → verb agrees with the nearer subject. The nearer subject (after 'nor') is 'the employees' which is plural. Therefore the verb must be plural: 'were present' not 'was present'. Error: 'was present' → should be 'were present'. Trap: Many students mistakenly make the verb agree with 'manager' (the first subject) — but the rule is proximity: agree with the NEARER/LAST subject.

questions.stem:
Find the part with a grammatical error:
(A) The news / (B) about the floods / (C) were shocking / (D) to everyone.
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'News' is an uncountable noun that always takes a singular verb, even though it ends in 's'. Error: 'were shocking' → should be 'was shocking'. Similarly: 'The news is good'; 'No news is good news'. Trap: 'news' looks plural (ends in -s) so students write 'were', but it is always singular in English (like 'mathematics', 'physics', 'economics').

questions.stem:
Find the part with a grammatical error:
(A) She has been / (B) working in this office / (C) since / (D) three years.
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Since' is used with a specific point in time (since 2020, since Monday). 'For' is used with a duration/period of time (for three years, for a month). Error: 'since three years' → should be 'for three years'. Rule: SINCE + point → SINCE 2020 / SINCE Monday / SINCE childhood. FOR + duration → FOR 3 years / FOR a week. Trap: Both 'since' and 'for' are used with perfect tenses, making the tense (has been) look correct — but the preposition itself is wrong.

questions.stem:
Find the part with a grammatical error:
(A) I am looking forward / (B) to meet / (C) the new / (D) team leader.
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Look forward to' is a phrasal verb where 'to' is a PREPOSITION (not part of an infinitive), so it must be followed by a gerund (V+ing), not a bare infinitive. Error: 'to meet' → should be 'to meeting'. Correct: 'I am looking forward to meeting the new team leader.' Trap: Students see 'to meet' and think it is the infinitive — but 'to' here is a preposition attached to the phrasal verb 'look forward to', which always requires a gerund.

questions.stem:
Find the part with a grammatical error:
(A) The thieves / (B) has already / (C) escaped / (D) before the police arrived.
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'The thieves' is plural, so the auxiliary verb must be plural: 'have', not 'has'. Error: 'has already' → should be 'had already'. (Furthermore, since both events are in the past and one happened BEFORE the other, the earlier event should use past perfect: 'had already escaped before the police arrived'.) The primary error examiners target is 'has' → 'had'. Trap: Even students who spot 'has/have' error might keep 'have escaped' instead of the more precise 'had escaped'.

questions.stem:
Find the part with a grammatical error:
(A) It is essential that / (B) every student / (C) submits their / (D) assignment on time.
questions.explanation: C is correct. After 'It is essential/important/necessary/vital that', English uses the SUBJUNCTIVE mood: bare infinitive (verb without -s/-es). Error: 'submits' → should be 'submit' (subjunctive). Full correct: 'It is essential that every student submit their assignment on time.' Note: 'their' is acceptable as a gender-neutral singular pronoun. Trap: Students see 'every student' (singular) and add -s to submit, thinking it agrees with the subject — but the subjunctive overrides subject-verb agreement after 'It is essential that'.

questions.stem:
Find the part with a grammatical error:
(A) She told me / (B) that she will attend / (C) the conference / (D) the following day.
questions.explanation: B is correct. Rule of backshift (sequence of tenses): when the reporting verb is in the past ('told'), the verb in the reported clause must shift back one tense. 'Will' (future simple) → 'would' (past of will). Error: 'will attend' → should be 'would attend'. Correct: 'She told me that she would attend the conference the following day.' Trap: 'The following day' (not 'next day') is already correct — it is the standard change in indirect speech for 'tomorrow'.

questions.stem:
Find the part with a grammatical error:
(A) Despite of / (B) his best efforts, / (C) he failed to / (D) clear the examination.
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Despite' is a preposition and is NEVER followed by 'of'. Error: 'Despite of' → should be 'Despite' (drop 'of'). Correct: 'Despite his best efforts, he failed to clear the examination.' Rule: Despite + noun/gerund (no 'of'). Compare: 'in spite of' (which DOES need 'of'). Trap: Students confuse 'despite' with 'in spite of' and write 'despite of' — extremely common SSC error.
